en: Hellas Central. The largest city on Mars. Population 800,000. An atmospheric dome. Inside was like Earth. Similar pressure. Similar oxygen. But Mars outside the windows was different. Red dust. A place humans couldn't survive. The dome maintained that boundary.

speaker: narrator
en: The city was divided into layers. Upper floors MCC administration. Middle floors engineer residences. Lower floors labor district. On Mars hierarchy was vertical. More dust the lower you went. Quieter the higher you went. Every hierarchy eventually took the same shape.

speaker: lifang
en: Orientation first. MCC standard new-arrival procedure.

speaker: lifang
en: Hellas Central layout. Emergency exit routes. Oxygen supply points. And who is who.

speaker: lifang
en: The last is most important.

speaker: narrator
en: A briefing room. Other new arrivals. Six of them. From different places. Different ships. But in the same room. People MCC had called. Different reasons each. Same destination. That was MCC's way.

speaker: lifang
en: MCC regulations. Read them. Within this week.

speaker: lifang
en: Oxygen allocation. Water allocation. Residential zone assignment. It's all in this book. Don't know it and you die. Can't pay the levy and you die. Same thing.

speaker: lifang
en: Questions?

speaker: lifang
en: Good if not. Ask when they come up later.

speaker: narrator
en: The regulations were thick. 247 pages. Someone had underlined them. A previous person's copy. The lines were thick. Important sections. Procedure for oxygen shortage. Emergency medical report channels. Those were heavily underlined. You could guess what the previous person had been through.

speaker: narrator
en: The first day ended. A residential zone was assigned. Middle level. There was a window. Through it the outer Hellas was visible. Beyond the dome. Red dust moving. Wind. The Martian wind made no sound. The dome blocked it. Wind visible but inaudible. Most things on Mars were like that.

speaker: narrator
en: Night came. The Martian night was long. 37 minutes longer than Earth. A day was 24 hours 37 minutes. For the first few days those 37 minutes felt strange. Feeling that strange things were strange was the first stage of adapting to Mars. The next was those strange things becoming normal.

speaker: lifang
en: Day two. Field tour. Follow me.

speaker: lifang
en: MCC Hellas Central facilities. Refinery. Administration building. Technical division. Medical facility. Mine operations center.

speaker: lifang
en: If a problem comes up anywhere, medical facility first. Then contact me. Don't reverse that order.

speaker: narrator
en: Outside the mine. A tunnel entrance. An elevator. Going down. 3 kilometers. Where miners went every day. Miners were coming up. A shift change. Faces caked in dust. Masks darker. They said nothing coming up. The silence of exhausted people.

speaker: narrator
en: One of the miners was young. About twenty. He lifted his mask. Just briefly. His face was visible. A tired face. Tiredness of that age. That age shouldn't be tired. But on Mars it didn't matter. The mine shaft was equal.

speaker: lifang
en: You were watching.

speaker: lifang
en: MCC new arrivals see the mine for the first time and react two ways. Uneasy, or feel nothing. You're a third thing.

speaker: lifang
en: No need to know what that is right now. Mars will tell you. It takes time.

speaker: narrator
en: Day three. Lifang gave documents. The first assignment. Sector 7 safety audit. Standard procedure. Field inspection. Write a report. Two-day deadline. Simple. That was how it started.

speaker: narrator
en: Sector 7. A small mining outpost on the outer Hellas. Staff 30. Primary mineral iron ore. A report form existed. A checklist. Safety equipment. Emergency exits. Oxygen backup. Checked one by one.

speaker: narrator
en: There was a problem. Not on the checklist. The ventilation system was old. No parts. Signs of improvised repair. Multiple times. Below standard. But formally it had passed. The checklist was designed to allow that.

speaker: narrator
en: More was there. Accident records. Past two years. Three cases. The cause section was blank. All three. Only names. Death. Death. Death. Deaths without cause. That was possible on Mars. If you didn't write the cause there was no cause.

speaker: lifang
en: How's the report.

speaker: lifang
en: Done?

speaker: lifang
en: Something's there. I can tell from your face. Three days on Mars and it shows on your face.

speaker: narrator
en: Told Lifang. The ventilation system. Accident records. Three deaths without cause. He listened. No expression. Still no expression after everything was said. The face of someone who had hidden expressions for a long time. That too was what Mars made.

speaker: lifang
en: I knew.

speaker: lifang
en: Nothing within MCC is unknown. Among what is known there are things said and things not said. Knowing the difference between those two is how you survive in this organization.

speaker: lifang
en: What will you write in the report.

speaker: narrator
en: Wrote the report. Wrote what was seen. Ventilation system. Aged parts. Improvised repairs. Blank cause of death. Three cases. The names. Wrote them. Didn't erase them. The first decision. The first decision on Mars. Mars would remember it.

speaker: lifang
en: Read it once more before submitting.

speaker: lifang
en: Once written there's no taking it back. Words written on Mars are carved in rock. MCC records everything. Remembers. Never erases.

speaker: lifang
en: Your decision.

speaker: narrator
en: Submitted. The report was submitted. Exactly as seen. Lifang took it. Read it. Slowly. When done he was still for a moment. That silence was long. But it didn't feel long. It was a silence worth waiting through.

speaker: lifang
en: Received.

speaker: lifang
en: Do you know where this report goes?

speaker: lifang
en: Chen Weiss's desk. Reports at this level all go there. Your name goes up there.

speaker: lifang
en: Remember that name. The most important name on Mars.

speaker: narrator
en: Day four. Hellas Central was becoming familiar. Memorized routes. Memorized faces. Masks made faces hard to memorize. So people memorized other things. Gait. Voice. The way they moved. Knowing people on Mars was like that.

speaker: narrator
en:
A red dot appeared beyond the window.
At first it looked like a star. As it grew closer — it became a planet.
Blood-red. Beautiful. Frightening. Now inside that planet. Seen from inside it was different. That was Mars's second face.

speaker: narrator
en:
Mars was waiting for you.
What would you become on this planet.
Chen Weiss would be reading the report. Holding her tea. Not drinking.

speaker: narrator
en: The stars didn't move. In space stars were always where they were. Only the ship moved. Cargo freighter Kariyope. Eighty thousand tons of freight. Forty-seven passengers. Under Captain Berk, twenty-three years in service, following the course toward Mars. The stars didn't know that.

speaker: narrator
en: The Kariyope drifted three more days before reaching Mars orbit. Navigator Berk didn't call it drifting. But his not calling it drifting didn't make it otherwise. The engines were efficient. The course was accurate. Still the arrival was late.

speaker: narrator
en: Arrivals are always late. That was one thing Berk had learned in twenty-three years. There were other things too but he hadn't written them down. There were more unwritten things than written ones.

speaker: narrator
en: The Kariyope's cargo hold was always filled with things returning from Mars. Scrap metal. Processed ore. Empty oxygen tanks. The next voyage would fill it again with the same things. Mars received and sent back. It didn't send people back.

speaker: narrator
en: This voyage's manifest. Two thousand eight hundred forty-seven items. Berk read half of it. The other half was always the same. The last entry was forty-seven passengers. Writing non-items as items was a navigator's job.

speaker: narrator
en: The vending machine was at the end of the corridor. Three drinks. Brown liquid. Different brown liquid. Yellowish brown liquid. Berk always chose the first. Called coffee. It wasn't coffee. But when he drank it Berk could pause for a moment. That was enough.

speaker: narrator
en: The Kariyope was entering Mars orbit. Final deceleration. Thirty-nine hours of it. There was nothing to do. Nothing that could be done was more accurate. Berk took a cup from the vending machine. He drank it. He could drink it. That was enough.

speaker: narrator
en: Twelve surveillance monitors. Berk could see all twelve at once. Old habit. Sector 1 sector 2 sector 3. The cargo hold. Engine room. Corridor. Dining cabin. Passenger cabin. Passenger cabin corner. Someone was there.

speaker: narrator
en: A small bag on the lap. A hand resting on top. The hand didn't move. Two days now. For two days Berk hadn't seen that hand move. Whether they were sleeping was unclear. The monitor resolution wasn't good.

speaker: narrator
en: Two days, Berk said to himself. No sleep. Standing at the vending machine. How far is Mars. Thirty-nine hours. That's survivable without sleep. Probably. He looked at the monitor again.

speaker: narrator
en: The name was on the manifest. Berk didn't look at it. People going to Mars often left their names behind. Sometimes they brought new ones. Either way it was the same to Berk.

speaker: narrator
en: One of the crew asked Berk. Is that person alright. Berk thought for a moment. Said yes. He didn't know precisely what alright meant but he said it anyway. People going to Mars were usually not alright. That's why they were going to Mars.

speaker: narrator
en: Dining cabin. Evening ration. Three of four rows full. Two mining families. Men who looked like engineers. A woman sitting alone. No expression. She ate. She didn't think about what the food tasted like. That too was a way of going to Mars.

speaker: narrator
en: A mining family's child dropped their tray. A sound. Everyone looked. The child didn't cry. The adult looked at the child. The child looked at the adult. No words. Mining children learned early. They learned before knowing what they were learning.

speaker: narrator
en: One person hadn't appeared at the dining cabin. A crewmember brought a ration tray. It wasn't accepted. The next day another tray. Also refused. On the third day no one brought one.

speaker: narrator
en: It was a seat without a window. The chosen seat. There was no desire to know Mars was out there. Not yet. When you get to Mars you'll see Mars.

speaker: narrator
en: The bag was heavy. It had always been heavy. Heavy since leaving Earth. Heavy even knowing what was inside. The weight wasn't about the contents.

speaker: narrator
en: There wasn't much in the bag. Even the owner didn't know everything that was in it. One old thing. What it was, there was no need to open the bag to know. The bag wasn't opened.

speaker: narrator
en: What would be on Mars. That question had ended long ago. There was no asking it now. On Mars there would be Mars. That was all. Whether that was enough could only be known by going there.

speaker: narrator
en: Whether there was somewhere to go or not, that was unknown too. There were people on Mars. That was known. Which direction to walk hadn't been decided. Decisions came after feet touched soil.

speaker: narrator
en: The Kariyope shuddered. Vibration from the deceleration. The cabin lights flickered. The hand still didn't move. Berk watched that hand for a long time. Then he looked away from the monitor and drank his coffee.

speaker: narrator
en: A small child from the mining family stirred awake. Slipped free from an adult's arm and wandered the cabin once. The adult didn't wake. The child returned. A hand in sleep closed around the child. The child slept again. The walls were thick. People were alone inside them.

speaker: narrator
en: Someone snored. Someone moaned. Someone whispered. Sleeping on a ship was different from sleeping on Earth. On the ship the ship kept moving. It didn't stop. That wasn't a bad thing. They were going to Mars. Whether going to Mars was a good thing was also unclear.

speaker: narrator
en: Berk went up to the observation deck. Four in the morning. No one on the deck. Stars through the glass. The stars didn't move. The ship was moving. Berk had felt this difference for twenty-three years. The difference was getting smaller.

speaker: narrator
en: The person was there too. Corner of the observation deck. The bag was on the floor. A hand rested on the strap. Not looking out the window. Eyes half-closed. It wasn't clear if they were sleeping. Berk didn't go in.

speaker: narrator
en: Berk went back to the corridor. One cup of brown liquid. He looked up at the ceiling. The ceiling was dark. Twenty-three years. Now Mars was twenty-two degrees off the right viewport. It was starting to look large.

speaker: narrator
en: An announcement. Six in the morning. Berk's voice. Approaching Mars. Beginning contact with Hellas control. Eighteen hours to arrival. Passengers please return to your seats and fasten your seatbelts.

speaker: narrator
en: People moved. Footsteps in the corridor. A child asked something. Is Mars visible. The adult answered. You'll see it soon. The child ran. Toward the window. The child's palms pressed against the glass.

speaker: narrator
en: No getting up from the seat. No going to the window. No desire to see Mars. Not yet. But knowing Mars was there. It was felt. The ship had changed. The sounds changed. The vibration changed. Mars was close.

speaker: narrator
en: Mars on the screen was a little larger. Blood-red. Like a sunset. But it wasn't a sunset. Mars was always like this. That was what Mars was. Someone said it was beautiful. There was no thought about beauty.

speaker: narrator
en: Berk exchanged communications with ground control. Kariyope. Hellas control. Requesting cargo clearance code. Hellas control responded. Code received. Protocol. Protocol that hadn't changed in twenty-three years.

speaker: berk
en: Is there a first-time Mars passenger among you.

speaker: berk
en: If it's your first time act like it's your second. Mars doesn't know the difference. Not knowing is the danger.

speaker: berk
en: Ten hours to Hellas Central. Everyone stay in your seats.

speaker: narrator
en: Ten hours. Those words remained. Ten hours. Whether it was long or short was unclear. It had taken six months to come from Earth to Mars. And ten hours felt far.

speaker: narrator
en: The ship tilted. Entry angle adjustment. Where the Martian atmosphere began. Red light came through the windows. The Martian atmosphere wrapped around the ship. Deceleration. Heat. Sound. That was how Mars received the ship.

speaker: narrator
en: The vibration intensified. The child cried. The adult held them. The engineers looked at each other. They all had experience. Still the vibration was heavy. The Kariyope was always like this. Berk knew. On the deceleration this ship made noise.

speaker: narrator
en: A hand rested on the bag. The hand didn't move. The ship shuddered. The shuddering wasn't unfelt. It wasn't that it wasn't felt. It was felt but not reacted to. The arrival was coming soon.

speaker: narrator
en: A red horizon appeared. The Hellas Basin. The lowest point on Mars. The deepest basin. People lived there. The child's palms pressed to the window turned red. It was Mars's light.

speaker: narrator
en: Hellas Central was visible below. Its size was hard to judge. It looked small. It grew larger as they got closer. Upon arrival it would be enormous. All buildings on Mars were like that. Small from outside, enormous inside. It should have been the other way around but wasn't.

speaker: narrator
en: Berk made an announcement. Prepare for landing. Seatbelts. All electronics off. Luggage under seats. Protocol. Twenty-three years of the same words. The voice hadn't changed. The content hadn't changed. Mars hadn't changed.

speaker: narrator
en: The landing runway was visible. Long concrete. Blood-red dust running across it. There was wind. Hellas always had wind. Small winds. Before a major storm the small winds always came first.

speaker: narrator
en: The Kariyope landed. Sand struck the windows. That was Mars's business. Impact. The ship stopped. The sound stopped. Quiet. The quiet of Mars. Different from the quiet of space. The quiet of Mars had something in it.

speaker: narrator
en: No one moved. Just a moment. The moment after landing. Everyone seemed to be confirming they were on Mars. When confirmed they would move. The child moved first. Children confirm quickly.

speaker: narrator
en: The airlock opened. Air came in. Recycled air. Purified Martian atmosphere. Low oxygen content. It would be dizzying at first. That too was protocol. Three days to adapt.

speaker: narrator
en: The mining family disembarked first. A child holding an adult's hand. The engineers came down. The woman alone. No expression. No expression for the entire voyage. No expression on Mars. Whether that was the right way was unknown.

speaker: narrator
en: Everyone disembarked. Last one remaining. The bag was lifted. Heavy. Walking down the aisle. Through the airlock. There were stairs. At the bottom of the stairs was Mars.

speaker: narrator
en: The soil of Mars was there beneath the first step. Under a blood-red sky. Hellas Central stood ahead. Enormous. Enormous even from outside. Inside it would be more enormous. Wind came. The bag was gripped tighter.

speaker: narrator
en: Berk was watching from the gangway above. Looking down at the people disembarking. Saw them all. He'd been seeing this for twenty-three years. The last person off stood with the bag and stopped. Looking at Hellas Central. Berk saw that too.

speaker: berk
en: Looks like that your first time.

speaker: berk
en: Looks like that your second time too. Third. You don't get used to it. That's Mars.

speaker: berk
en: Where are you going.

speaker: narrator
en: Where to go was unknown. There was no answer to that question. No answer was given. Berk was expected to ask again. He didn't. That was Berk's way. On Mars not answering was an answer.

speaker: narrator
en: Hellas Central. Standing before it. Inside the building something was running. Things that didn't stop. To the right was MCC. To the left was the labor district. Straight ahead the main hall. Behind was the Kariyope. The Kariyope would leave in six hours.

speaker: narrator
en: Six hours. A return was possible. Some people came to Mars and turned back. Berk knew about them. People like that existed. They too set foot on Mars. That was enough for them. Those for whom it wasn't enough stayed.

speaker: narrator
en: The bag wasn't set down. Setting it down made it a decision. Holding it still meant not yet. People walked past. Miners. Engineers. Everyone going somewhere. They all had somewhere to go.

speaker: narrator
en:
The Kariyope left six hours later. Berk checked the manifest. The last name to disembark was there. Berk didn't read that name. A name on Mars began here. Different from the Kariyope's manifest.

The soil of Mars was beneath the feet.
The blood-red sky was above.
Somewhere was walked toward.
